report:
## Conclusion

**The claim is false.** The scientific consensus, based on direct physiological measurements, is that wearing cloth or surgical masks—even for prolonged periods—does not cause dangerous carbon dioxide (CO2) buildup or hypoxia in healthy people or in most patients with lung disease.

Controlled studies measuring blood gases directly found no meaningful differences in oxygen or CO2 levels with or without a mask, including in patients with COPD (severely damaged lungs) ([Fox News summary of gas-exchange study](https://www.foxnews.com/health/face-masks-dont-cause-carbon-dioxide-build-up-or-restrict-breathing)). While CO2 concentration *inside the mask's air pocket* can rise slightly above ambient air (measured at a few thousand ppm versus ~500-900 ppm unmasked), this localized increase does not translate into a meaningful rise in blood CO2, because masks are not airtight and normal breathing still exchanges gas efficiently with the surrounding air ([AAQR study](https://aaqr.org/articles/aaqr-20-07-covid-0403.pdf)).

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of N95 and surgical masks confirmed that N95 masks may raise CO2 slightly more than surgical masks during activity, but overall there was no clinically significant difference from wearing no mask at all ([PMC meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11386028/)).

Multiple independent fact-checking organizations (AFP, Reuters, AP, USA Today) reached the same conclusion after consulting health experts and reviewing evidence, rating the "masks cause hypercapnia" claim false or misleading ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/05/30/fact-check-wearing-face-mask-not-cause-hypoxia-hypercapnia/5260106002/)).

Symptoms sometimes attributed to CO2 poisoning (headache, lightheadedness) from mask-wearing are more plausibly explained by heat, humidity, anxiety, or restricted airflow discomfort—not hazardous gas buildup.
